query: Many physical and chemical fabrication approaches have produced multi-element, near-equiatomic solid-solution nanoparticles, yet their synthesis–structure–property relationships remain poorly established. This limits evaluation of their suitability for catalytic operation at 773–1173 K and thermoelectric use at 473–1923 K, including catalytic settings where low noble-metal content is desirable. What governs whether these nanoparticles preserve structural and chemical stability under such service regimes, and why? Formulate one testable mechanistic hypothesis, specify a controlled intervention that separates it from competing explanations, predict observations relative to a baseline, define its boundary conditions, connect it to the prior evidence summarized above, and provide a clear falsification test.

generation.hypothesis: High configurational entropy in near‐equiatomic multi‐element nanoparticles creates a 'sluggish diffusion' effect that impedes atomic rearrangements and phase segregation, thereby preserving structural integrity and chemical composition under service conditions.
generation.material_initial_state: Uniformly mixed, near‐equiatomic, solid‐solution nanoparticles with homogeneously distributed multiple metal elements.
generation.intervention: Prepare two nanoparticle sets: one with near‐equiatomic (high-entropy) composition and the other intentionally off‐equiatomic to reduce configurational entropy, while keeping all other synthesis conditions constant.
generation.conditions: Expose both sets to service-relevant thermal conditions: catalytic operation at 773–1173 K and thermoelectric operation at 473–1923 K under controlled atmospheres.
generation.structural_mediator: Local atomic arrangements that elevate diffusion barriers—i.e., the sluggish diffusion mechanism—which delays grain growth, phase separation, and surface compositional changes.
generation.mechanism: The high entropy raises the activation energy for atomic migration, suppressing processes such as phase segregation and sintering that typically degrade catalyst and thermoelectric performance at elevated temperatures.
generation.predicted_outcome: High-entropy (near-equiatomic) nanoparticles will display significantly less grain growth, phase segregation, and surface compositional changes compared to their off-equiatomic counterparts, maintaining their catalytic activity and thermoelectric properties closer to the initial baseline.
generation.baseline: Nanoparticles with reduced configurational entropy (off-equiatomic) that are expected to show accelerated atomic diffusion and pronounced structural and chemical degradation when exposed to the same thermal conditions.
generation.boundary: This mechanism is expected to dominate under the specified thermal regimes (773–1173 K for catalytic use and 473–1923 K for thermoelectric use) in inert or controlled atmospheres; effects might differ with additional variables such as reactive gas environments or extreme pressures.
generation.uncertainty: Exact thresholds for onset of significant sluggish diffusion and the interplay with other factors (e.g., support interactions, partial oxidation) remain to be quantitatively established through systematic study.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize two sets of nanoparticles with identical processing conditions: one set with near‐equiatomic (high-entropy) composition and another set with a deliberately off‐equiatomic composition to lower configurational entropy. Subject both sets to standardized high-temperature treatments matching the catalytic and thermoelectric regimes. Pre- and post-treatment, use transmission electron microscopy (TEM), X-ray diffraction (XRD), and X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) to characterize grain size, phase composition, and surface chemistry. Additionally, assess catalytic and/or thermoelectric performance.
measurements: Catalytic activity or thermoelectric performance over time
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the off-equiatomic (lower-entropy) nanoparticles exhibit no statistically significant increase in structural degradation, phase segregation, or performance decline compared to the near-equiatomic (high-entropy) nanoparticles after thermal exposure, then the hypothesis that high configurational entropy (via sluggish diffusion) governs stability is falsified.

Strengthening in multi-principal element alloys with local-chemical-order roughened dislocation pathways

Abstract: High-entropy and medium-entropy alloys are presumed to have a configurational entropy as high as that of an ideally mixed solid solution (SS) of multiple elements in near-equal proportions. However, enthalpic interactions inevitably render such chemically disordered SSs rare and metastable, except at very high temperatures. Here we highlight the wide variety of local chemical ordering (LCO) that sets these concentrated SSs apart from traditional solvent-solute ones. Using atomistic simulations, we reveal that the LCO of the multi-principal-element NiCoCr SS changes with alloy processing conditions, producing a wide range of generalized planar fault energies. We show that the LCO heightens the ruggedness of the energy landscape and raises activation barriers governing dislocation activities. This influences the selection of dislocation pathways in slip, faulting, and twinning, and increases the lattice friction to dislocation motion via a nanoscale segment detrapping mechanism. Kinetically-controlled laser-synthesis of colloidal high-entropy alloy nanoparticles†

Abstract: AbstractThe single-step incorporation of multiple immiscible elements into colloidal high-entropy alloy (HEA) nanoparticles has manifold technological potential, but it continues to be a challenge for state-of-the-art synthesis methods. Hence, the development of a synthesis approach by which the chemical composition and phase of colloidal HEA nanoparticles can be controlled could lead to a new pool of nanoalloys with unparalleled functionalities. Herein, this study reports the single-step synthesis of colloidal CoCrFeMnNi HEA nanoparticles with targeted equimolar stoichiometry and diameters less than 5 nm by liquid-phase, ultrashort-pulsed laser ablation of the consolidated and heat-treated micropowders of the five constituent metals. Further, the scalability of the process with an unprecedented productivity of 3 grams of colloidal HEA nanoparticles per hour is demonstrated. Electrochemical analysis reveals a unique redox behavior of the particles' surfaces in an alkaline environment and a potential for future application as a heterogeneous catalyst for the oxygen evolution reaction.
